overview.title: What he takes on.
overview.text: Car wrecks, truck crashes and falls on someone else's property lead the practice. Each has its own deadlines, and its own evidence that disappears first.

services.title: Truck & 18-Wheeler Accidents
services.text: Commercial carriers, logbooks and federal safety rules. A collision with an 18-wheeler is not a bigger car wreck.
services.lead: A collision with an 18-wheeler is not a bigger car wreck. Commercial carriers are governed by federal safety regulations, they carry policies an order of magnitude larger than a private driver, and they have a rapid-response team whose job is to limit what the case is worth before you have spoken to anyone.
services.imageAlt: An 18-wheeler on the highway at dawn

covers.title: Evidence that has a deadline
covers.text: The work starts immediately: preserving the electronic control module, the driver's hours-of-service logs, maintenance records, and the dashcam footage a carrier is under no obligation to keep once the retention window closes.

covers.title: What we look for
covers.text: Hours-of-service violations and falsified logbooks. Negligent hiring and retention. Improper loading or securement. Deferred maintenance on brakes and tyres.

covers.title: The carrier's own safety record
covers.text: A carrier's record often shows the collision was not the first of its kind.

covers.title: The insurance side
covers.text: David spent time as an adjuster for a large insurer before he practised law. He knows how a commercial claim is reserved, what the carrier's own investigators are told to document, and where the valuation gets quietly reduced.

services.title: Car & Rideshare Accidents
services.summary: Uninsured motorists, Uber and Lyft, hit-and-run.
services.text: Uninsured motorists, Uber and Lyft, hit-and-run. The first offer is not the value of your case.
services.lead: An early offer is made before anyone knows the full extent of your injuries, before treatment has run its course, and before the lost income is countable. It is made because it is cheap, not because it is fair. We do not send a demand until we know what the medical picture actually is.

covers.title: What the first week decides
covers.text: Most of what proves a case has a retention window — onboard data, footage, incident reports. Once it closes, the argument becomes one word against another.

covers.title: Rideshare claims
covers.text: Uber and Lyft carry substantial coverage, but which policy applies turns on what the driver was doing at the moment of the collision — offline, waiting for a request, en route, or carrying a passenger. Getting that period wrong can cost the entire claim.

covers.title: Uninsured and hit-and-run
covers.text: Texas has a significant uninsured driver population. If the at-fault driver has no coverage or cannot be found, your own uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage may be the claim — and your insurer becomes, in practical terms, the opposing party.

services.title: Motorcycle Accidents
services.summary: Where bias against the rider decides the offer.
services.text: Where bias against the rider decides the offer, and the file has to be built for a jury from the beginning.
services.lead: Adjusters and jurors carry an assumption that the rider was speeding, weaving, or reckless — often before a single fact is heard. That assumption gets priced into the offer.

covers.title: Overcoming the assumption
covers.text: Scene reconstruction, sight-line analysis, and a file built from the beginning for a jury rather than for a settlement conference.

covers.title: Injuries are rarely minor
covers.text: Without a cage there is little between the rider and the road. Orthopaedic injuries, road rash requiring grafts, and traumatic brain injury are common, and the long-term cost is routinely underestimated in an early demand.

covers.title: What the first week decides
covers.text: Most of what proves a case has a retention window — onboard data, footage, incident reports. Once it closes, the argument becomes one word against another.

services.title: Premises Liability
services.text: Falls, unsafe property and negligent security, where the duty owed turns on your status as a visitor.
services.lead: Texas sorts visitors into invitees, licensees and trespassers, and the duty owed differs for each. A customer in a store is owed considerably more than a social guest. Establishing status correctly is the first fight.

covers.title: Notice is the second fight
covers.text: It is rarely enough that a hazard existed. The question is whether the owner knew or should have known about it and failed to act. Incident reports, inspection logs and surveillance footage answer that — and all three have retention windows.

covers.title: Negligent security
covers.text: Where a foreseeable criminal act occurs on poorly secured property, the owner may share responsibility. These cases turn on the history of the location and what the owner did in response to it.

services.title: Work & Offshore Injuries
services.text: Construction, maritime and Jones Act claims, including the routes that sit outside the compensation system entirely.
services.lead: On a construction site or offshore, who is responsible is rarely only your employer, and the route to a claim depends on which system the work falls under.

covers.title: Non-subscriber employers
covers.text: An employer who opts out of the workers' compensation system loses the immunity that comes with it. That can open a direct negligence claim against the employer — a route not available in most states.

covers.title: Third-party claims
covers.text: On a construction site, responsibility often lies with a party other than your employer: a general contractor, a subcontractor, an equipment manufacturer, or a property owner. Those claims sit outside the compensation system entirely.

covers.title: Offshore and the Jones Act
covers.text: Seamen injured in the course of their work fall under the Jones Act rather than state law, with its own standards and its own deadlines. Gulf work makes this a live question for Houston-area workers.

services.title: Wrongful Death
services.summary: He wrote the Texas Bar CLE paper on these.
services.text: Wrongful death and survival claims, an area David has authored and presented State Bar of Texas material on.
services.lead: Under Texas law the surviving spouse, children and parents may bring a wrongful death action. A survival claim, which belongs to the estate, is separate and covers what the person themselves endured before death. The two are often brought together and are valued differently.

covers.title: Written on, not just practised
covers.text: David authored and presented continuing legal education material for the State Bar of Texas on wrongful death, and on auto collision litigation. It is an area he has taught to other lawyers.

covers.title: What we ask of you
covers.text: Very little, at first. There is no version of this where paperwork should be your problem. We will tell you plainly whether there is a claim, and if there is not, we will tell you that too.

steps.title: Tell us what happened
steps.text: A few sentences, a photo, a police report — whatever you have. It costs nothing and it is not a commitment.

steps.title: We go and get the evidence
steps.text: Onboard data, logbooks, surveillance, incident reports. Most of it has a retention window, which is why the first week matters.

steps.title: We make them value it properly
steps.text: David worked as an adjuster. The file gets built so the other side has to treat it as a trial risk, not a nuisance.

steps.title: You decide
steps.text: Settle or go to trial. It is your call, made with a straight account of what each road is worth.

about.title: He worked for the insurance company.
text: A fifth-generation Texan, born and raised in San Marcos, who learned how claims are valued from inside the company that pays them. While he was in law school, David worked as an insurance adjuster for a large insurance company, and as a private investigator.

He knows how a claim is reserved, what an adjuster is instructed to document, which injuries get quietly discounted, and what a file has to look like before an insurer treats it as a trial risk rather than a nuisance.

David is the sole founding member of the firm. Our case managers keep things moving, while David stays directly involved in the strategy and resolution of your case. The firm has been practising under this mark since 2011.

faqs.q: What does the case review cost?
faqs.a: Nothing. It costs nothing to find out where you stand, and the review is free and confidential. A person reads every message.

faqs.q: Do you only take cases in Houston?
faqs.a: No. David takes cases from across the United States and is not restricted to a particular county or state. The firm evaluates each matter on its facts, not on whether it began inside a short list of Texas counties.
Sí. Desde la primera llamada hasta el final de su caso, lo atendemos en su idioma. La evaluación es gratis y confidencial.

faqs.q: Why does the first week matter so much?
faqs.a: Most of what proves a case has a retention window — onboard data, logbooks, surveillance, incident reports. Once it closes, the argument becomes one word against another.

faqs.q: Should I accept the first offer?
faqs.a: An early offer is made before anyone knows the full extent of your injuries, before treatment has run its course, and before the lost income is countable. It is made because it is cheap, not because it is fair.

faqs.q: Does contacting you create an attorney-client relationship?
faqs.a: No. Using the website, viewing information on it, sending an email, calling the firm or submitting an online form does not by itself create an attorney-client relationship. One is established only when the firm agrees to represent you and the necessary engagement requirements have been satisfied.

facts.heading: Results
facts.text: The firm's largest settlements include $33,000,000 in a trucking accident and $11,797,000 for a workplace incident, alongside settlements of $12,000,000, $11,900,000, $11,750,000 and $8,292,000. Sixty-three settled cases are on record, each with its case type, county, year and outcome. Every case is different, and prior results do not guarantee a similar outcome.

facts.heading: Deadlines to know
items: Car, truck, motorcycle and premises claims must be filed within two years in Texas.
A wrongful death claim must be filed within two years of the date of death, and the wrongful death and survival claims are brought separately.
Most Texas work injury claims must be filed within two years, and a Jones Act claim within three.
A commercial carrier must hold at least $750,000 in coverage under federal rules, and a truck's onboard data can be overwritten within days.
Texas sorts property visitors into three classes, and each is owed a different duty.
The case review is free.

facts.heading: The practice
facts.text: Six areas of catastrophic injury work. Each one has its own deadlines, its own regulators, and its own evidence that disappears first — which is why the first week matters more than most people are told.
